prompt: Benzoyl chloride reacts with sodium acetate, CH3CO2^− Na+, in ether. What is the organic product?

choices.text: Acetic benzoic anhydride
Benzoic anhydride
choices.why: The symmetrical benzoic anhydride would need benzoate as the nucleophile. Acetate gives an unsymmetrical anhydride.

choices.text: Methyl benzoate
choices.why: An ester would need an alcohol or alkoxide. Here a carboxylate oxygen bonds to the benzoyl carbon.

choices.text: Phenyl acetate
choices.why: Phenyl acetate, CH3CO2C6H5, is an ester with one carbonyl group. The product here has two acyl groups joined through an oxygen.

explanation: Acid anhydrides are typically prepared by nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acid chloride by a carboxylate anion. Acetate displaces chloride from benzoyl chloride, giving the unsymmetrical acetic benzoic anhydride.

prompt: How does the chemistry of acid anhydrides compare with that of acid chlorides?

choices.text: It is similar, but anhydrides react more slowly
It is similar, but anhydrides react faster
choices.why: Anhydrides are less reactive than acid chlorides, so they react more slowly.

choices.text: Anhydrides don't react with water, alcohols, or amines
choices.why: Anhydrides react with water to form acids, with alcohols to form esters, and with amines to form amides.

choices.text: Anhydrides react only with lithium diorganocopper reagents
choices.why: Diorganocopper reagents react only with acid chlorides, not with anhydrides.

explanation: The chemistry of acid anhydrides is similar to that of acid chlorides, although anhydrides react more slowly. They react with water to form acids, with alcohols to form esters, with amines to form amides, and with LiAlH4 to form primary alcohols.

prompt: Which reactions of acid anhydrides are commonly used?

choices.text: Only the ester-forming and amide-forming reactions
Only hydrolysis to carboxylic acids
choices.why: Anhydrides do react with water, but the reactions commonly used are ester and amide formation.

choices.text: Only LiAlH4 reduction to primary alcohols
choices.why: Anhydrides are reduced by LiAlH4, but this isn't one of the commonly used reactions.

choices.text: Only Grignard reactions to tertiary alcohols
choices.why: The section lists ester and amide formation as the commonly used reactions of anhydrides.

explanation: Acid anhydrides undergo hydrolysis, alcoholysis, aminolysis, and reduction, but only the ester- and amide-forming reactions are commonly used. Acetic anhydride is the usual example.

prompt: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is made commercially by treating salicylic acid (o-hydroxybenzoic acid) with acetic anhydride. What happens in this reaction?

choices.text: The –OH group on the ring is acetylated, giving an acetate ester
The –CO2H group is converted into an N-substituted amide
choices.why: No amine is involved, so no amide can form. The ring –OH acts as an alcohol and is acetylated.

choices.text: The –CO2H group is reduced to a –CH2OH group by the anhydride
choices.why: Acetic anhydride isn't a reducing agent. It transfers an acetyl group.

choices.text: The –OH group on the ring is replaced by a chlorine atom
choices.why: There is no chlorine in the reaction. The by-product is acetate ion.

explanation: Acetic anhydride is often used to prepare acetate esters from alcohols. Aspirin is made by acetylating the –OH group of o-hydroxybenzoic acid, with acetate ion as the by-product.

prompt: Acetaminophen is made from p-hydroxyaniline, HOC6H4NH2, and acetic anhydride. Which group reacts, and why?

choices.text: The –NH2 group, because it is more nucleophilic than the –OH group
The –OH group, because it is more nucleophilic than the –NH2 group
choices.why: The –NH2 group is the more nucleophilic one, so it reacts and the –OH does not.

choices.text: Both groups, at equal rates, giving a product with two acetyl groups
choices.why: Only the more nucleophilic –NH2 group reacts. Acetaminophen has one acetyl group, on nitrogen.

choices.text: The –NH2 group, because it is a better leaving group than –OH
choices.why: The –NH2 group is the nucleophile here, not a leaving group. Acetate ion is the leaving group.

explanation: Acetic anhydride is commonly used to prepare N-substituted acetamides from amines. With p-hydroxyaniline, only the more nucleophilic –NH2 group reacts, not the less nucleophilic –OH group, giving acetaminophen.

prompt: In the reaction of p-hydroxyaniline with acetic anhydride to give acetaminophen, what is the leaving group?

choices.text: Acetate ion
Hydroxide ion
choices.why: The ring –OH group isn't involved. The anhydride loses one of its acetate halves.

choices.text: Chloride ion
choices.why: There is no chlorine in an anhydride. Chloride is the leaving group from acid chlorides.

choices.text: Amide ion, ^−NH2
choices.why: The nitrogen is the nucleophile and stays bonded in acetaminophen.

explanation: This is a typical nucleophilic acyl substitution, with p-hydroxyaniline as the nucleophile and acetate ion as the leaving group (Exercise 21.5.1).

prompt: Why are acid chlorides normally preferred over anhydrides for introducing acyl groups other than acetyl?

choices.text: Only half of each anhydride is used; the other half is a by-product
Anhydrides react faster than acid chlorides and are hard to control
choices.why: Anhydrides react more slowly than acid chlorides.

choices.text: Anhydrides can't react with alcohols or amines at all, only with water
choices.why: Anhydrides react with both. Ester and amide formation are their most common uses.

choices.text: Anhydrides always give tertiary alcohols instead of esters or amides
choices.why: Anhydrides give esters with alcohols and amides with amines. Tertiary alcohols come from Grignard reactions.

explanation: In anhydride reactions only half of the molecule is used, while the other half acts as the leaving group and becomes a by-product (acetate ion for acetic anhydride). Anhydrides are therefore inefficient, so acid chlorides are normally used for acyl groups other than acetyl.

prompt: When acetic anhydride acetylates an amine, how many of its two acetyl groups end up in the amide product?
explanation: Only one acetyl group is transferred. The other half of the anhydride acts as the leaving group and becomes acetate ion. That is why the section calls anhydrides inefficient.

prompt: Phthalic anhydride (1,2-benzenedicarboxylic anhydride) is a cyclic anhydride. What product forms when it reacts with one equivalent of methanol?

choices.text: The monomethyl ester: one –CO2CH3 group and one –CO2H group on the ring
Dimethyl phthalate, with two –CO2CH3 groups on the ring
choices.why: Only one equivalent of methanol is used, and only one carbonyl group reacts with it.

choices.text: Phthalic acid, with two –CO2H groups on the ring, plus methyl acetate
choices.why: No acetyl groups are present. Methanol becomes part of an ester on the ring; it isn't lost as methyl acetate.

choices.text: Methyl benzoate plus a separate molecule of formic acid
choices.why: No carbon–carbon bond breaks. Both carbonyl carbons stay attached to the ring.

explanation: Methanol attacks one carbonyl group and the other half of the anhydride is the leaving group. Because the anhydride is cyclic, that leaving group stays in the same molecule as a carboxyl group, giving the monomethyl ester of benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (Exercise 21.5.2).

prompt: What amide forms when methylamine, CH3NH2, reacts with acetic anhydride?

choices.text: N-Methylacetamide, CH3CONHCH3
Acetamide, CH3CONH2
choices.why: The nitrogen keeps its methyl group, so the product is an N-substituted acetamide.

choices.text: N,N-Dimethylacetamide, CH3CON(CH3)2
choices.why: Methylamine has only one methyl group to bring to the nitrogen.

choices.text: N-Methylpropanamide, CH3CH2CONHCH3
choices.why: The acyl group transferred from acetic anhydride is acetyl, with two carbons.

explanation: Acetic anhydride is commonly used to prepare N-substituted acetamides from amines. The amine nitrogen replaces an acetate group on one acyl carbon, giving CH3CONHCH3 and acetate ion.
